daysW4.title: Hontanas -> Itero de la Vega
daysW4.short_desc: Meseta day 3. Friends from All a round the World, a steep climb, and pilgrim inner with Paula
daysW4.long_desc: We stayed at the charming Villa Fontanas in the small village of Hontanas, a pleasant surprise along the Camino. Last night, we enjoyed a wonderful dinner with our Camino friends: Daniel from San Diego, a Lexie from Melbourne, a man from Flensburg in Germany, Max from Bristol, and a woman from Ireland. Laughter, stories, and true Camino spirit filled the evening. Today’s walk took us through Castrojeriz, a picturesque village we had actually visited back in 2022 during a “try-out” pilgrimage trip with Rolfs Resor. After leaving town, we faced a fairly steep one-kilometer climb, short, but intense! We had to hurry to reach Itero de la Vega by 3:00 p.m. sharp, as we had made a reservation and didn’t want to risk losing it. We made it with five minutes to spare, a small but satisfying victory. Even with a booking, punctuality is key during this busy season on the Camino. Have to do it the Spanish way. In the evening, we were treated to a delicious pilgrim dinner, lovingly prepared by our host Paula. We dined with Laura & Adam, who run a YouTube channel about the Camino, along with fellow pilgrims from Denmark, Germany, the UK, and Australia. Great food, great company and yet another day that reminds us why we’re walking. It’s the people and pilgrims you meet along the way that truly make the Camino unforgettabl!

daysW4.title: Itero de la Vega -> Frómista
daysW4.short_desc: Familiar faces, a quiet town, and the Less glamorous side of the Camino
daysW4.long_desc: We set off from our albergue in Itero de la Vega early in the morning. With only about 250 residents, the village didn’t have much to offer. In fact, it was a bit sad to see several abandoned and crumbling houses, something not uncommon in rural inland Spain. About 8 kilometers later, we reached Boadilla del Camino, where we stopped for a coffee and sandwich. Just as we were about to continue, we ran into a familiar face from the Pyrenees, Ted from Washington, D.C.! We had met him on our first night in Orisson, and again about a week ago. These kinds of reunions are part of what makes the Camino so special. Ted had some unfortunate news. Jenny from Canberra, another pilgrim we met early on, had developed infected blisters and might have to end her Camino early. A reminder that the Camino, for all its beauty, is also a serious physical challenge. Eventually, we arrived in Frómista, where we checked into a simple but comfortable hotel. Unfortunately, it didn’t offer dinner or breakfast and the town itself felt rather dull. We had expected more, since Frómista is a known stop for many pilgrims, but the services were surprisingly limited. In the end, we managed to find a small bar where we bought a slice of pizza. Some days on the Camino are full of wonder, others are simply about getting through and finding a place to rest.

daysW4.title: Frómista -> Carrión de los Condes
daysW4.short_desc: From Canal walk to Monastery Hotel and Halfway point in Carrión de los Condes!
daysW4.long_desc: Before leaving Frómista, we want to highlight the lovely Canal de Castilla you pass just before entering the town. It offers a peaceful walk along the water, and to our surprise, there even seems to be some kind of canal boat traffic, a charming detail in the heart of the Castilian countryside. We began today’s walk toward Carrión de los Condes around 8:30 a.m. The trail followed alongside the main road for most of the way and not the most varied stretch, but easy to walk. The morning was chilly, but by 11:00, the sun had begun to warm the path, just as we’ve come to expect. Already at the entrance to Carrión de los Condes, we noticed a livelier atmosphere and more people, open cafés, and a gentle city buzz that felt refreshing after the quieter Meseta villages. We instantly liked the town’s inviting vibe, with plenty of outdoor seating and small squares to explore. Our hotel was at the far end of town, the stunning Hotel Real Monasterio de San Zoilo, a former monastery beautifully transformed into a hotel. A place full of history and tranquility. Here, we celebrated reaching the halfway point of our Camino, with a glass of Cava in the sun. We ended the day with a truly delicious dinner, a tomato and burrata salad to start, followed by a cod loin with ratatouille as the main course. A perfect way to mark that we are now halfway to Santiago de Compostela.
daysW4.accommodation: Hotel Real Monasterio de san Zoilo

daysW4.title: Carrión de los Condes -> Ledigos
daysW4.short_desc: A never-ending straight path, three food trucks, and a surprisingly good stay
daysW4.long_desc: Today’s walk from Carrión de los Condes to Ledigos was one we had been slightly dreading, the infamous 17-kilometer straight stretch with no villages, no shade, and little variation. A true mental challenge, especially out here on the Meseta where the horizon seems to never get closer.This is dag 6 on the Meseta! Thankfully, we had heard there would be food trucks along the way and that turned out to be true! We came across three in total. The first was more of a coffee stand, while the other two offered light lunch options. We managed to enjoy both a coffee break and a small lunch, which made the stretch a bit more bearable. Still, the path felt long, monotonous, hot and mentally exhausting. About halfway, a Danish couple in our age passed us at a fast pace. They were aiming for 30 kilometers today. We were more than happy with our 24 km. Around 4 p.m., we reached Ledigos and checked in at the lovely La Morena albergue. Right away, we could see that all the glowing reviews on Booking were well deserved. The place felt new, clean, very welcoming and with fruit, water, and even foot cream in the room. A small detail that made a big difference. We ended the day with a pilgrim dinner where we could choose from several options. It was perfectly decent and after a day like this, that’s all we needed.

daysW4.title: Ledigos-> Sahagún
daysW4.short_desc: Meseta day 7.Toward Sahagún, new encounters and a shorter Stage
daysW4.long_desc: We left the lovely La Morena albergue in the morning sunshine and continued our walk. Everything was great, except for the breakfast, which seems to be the case almost everywhere (unless you’re staying at one of the nicer hotels). In the next village, we stopped for a coffee break and met two friendly pilgrims from Estonia, Kadri and Katlin. They’re walking just part of the Camino and plan to finish in Astorga, the end of the Meseta. As always, these brief encounters spark good conversations about the road, the weather, and life. Today’s walk was shorter than usual, which felt just right after several long days. We arrived early in Sahagún, had lunch in the center, and headed to our hotel, which turned out to be better than expected. Sahagún (population around 2,800) is another town that was powerful and prominent during the 1100s, but today shows signs of time passing, with some crumbling buildings and abandoned homes alongside its history and charm. We ended the day with dinner at the hotel, which was perfectly fine, nothing special, but satisfying. A quiet, easy day on the Camino and just what we needed.

daysW4.title: Sahagún-> El Burgo Ranero
daysW4.short_desc: Leaving Sahagún and another day (day 8) on the Endless Meseta
daysW4.long_desc: We left Sahagún early in the morning and headed out into yet another day across the open expanse of the Meseta. There’s something unique about this vast, stark landscape, but after so many days, we’re beginning to feel the mental fatigue, not just in our legs but in our spirits. It’s easy to understand why some pilgrims choose to skip sections of the Meseta, especially those who’ve walked the Camino before and know exactly what lies ahead. While the horizon has its own quiet beauty, the mental challenge can be just as demanding as the physical one. Now, we’re counting down the days until we reach León on Monday, our next major destination, and a welcome return to city life after the long, solitary rhythm of the plains.
descriptions_gallery: Never too late to give up!

daysW4.title: El Burgo Ranero -> Mansilla de las Mulas
daysW4.short_desc: Meseta day 9. It’s the People Who Bring El Camino Francés to Life
daysW4.long_desc: The landscapes are beautiful and some times endless, the history is rich, and the path El Camino Francés is well know and worn, but it’s the people and the pilgrims you meet along the way that truly make the Camino unforgettable. Pilgrims from all over the world, with different backgrounds, languages, ages, and reasons for walking, yet all heading in the same direction to Santiago de Compostela. It’s through conversations, shared meals, smiles, and unexpected reunions that El Camino Francés reveals its soul. Every encounter holds a story, every meal builds connection, and every “Buen Camino” is a small reminder of the shared journey that makes this pilgrimage so meaningful.
daysW4.accommodation: Hotel Rural La Casa de los Soportales
